cards.title: Pre-launch asset preparation checklist
cards.summary: Prepare logo, favicon, colors, fonts and product/collection assets before touching the Shopify theme to avoid rework.
cards.use_when: You are about to build or rebuild a Shopify storefront and need to decide what to gather before starting theme customization.
steps: Prepare a logo as a transparent-background PNG (remove background with Canva, CapCut, or an AI background remover if you only have a colored-background version).
Prepare a square favicon - the small icon shown in the browser tab; a single brand letter is enough, keep it simple.

Lock a palette of four or five hex colors containing both dark and light values so you have contrast flexibility later in design; choose colors that make sense for the niche (blues for water-related products, greens for nature-related ones).

Choose one or two fonts from the Shopify font library, not custom fonts, since non-Shopify fonts require custom coding and a developer; check the same or a similar font exists in Canva so social content matches the store.
Prepare product list, collection list, product photos, lifestyle photos, and the About Us copy before building, since having them ready makes store work substantially easier.
caveats: Custom fonts are possible but need a hired developer to implement.
The source presents the four-to-five-color rule as a working habit, not an enforced standard.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choosing a Shopify plan by card rate and staff seats
cards.summary: Compare Basic, Grow and Advanced on card rates, staff seats and global/market features, and check legacy accounts separately.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which Shopify plan to subscribe to, or whether upgrading will pay for itself at your current sales volume.
steps: Compare the card rates the source cites: Basic 1.5%, Grow 1.3%, Advanced 1.1% on store payments - the main difference between tiers in this account.
Estimate your monthly processed sales and check whether the rate saving on the higher tier exceeds the price difference before upgrading purely for rates.
Check staff seats: Basic allows roughly one to two users, Grow up to five, Advanced up to 15; if multiple people must manage orders or the storefront, factor that in.
Check whether you sell into multiple markets or need global settings; the source says market/global features differ by tier, so international sellers may need Grow or Advanced.
Treat Shopify Plus separately: it is the only plan that allows customizing the Shopify checkout page, and the source cites roughly $2,000-$2,300/month - relevant only at an advanced stage.

If your store is old, open Settings and audit which features you actually have: the source reports legacy accounts were migrated with varying entitlements, so an old Grow account may or may not include global settings.
Verify plan pricing, card rates and seat limits in the current Shopify admin before committing, since these change.
caveats: The 1.5/1.3/1.1% card rates are the source's figures at recording time; verify current rates.
Plan names, seat counts and Plus pricing are the source's account and may have since changed.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Store details, currency, and order numbering configuration
cards.summary: Set store name, contact email, billing region, currency and order ID settings so customer-facing notifications and localization are correct.
cards.use_when: You are in Shopify Settings > General during initial store setup and need to configure identity, currency and order numbering.
steps: Under General > Store details, set the store name exactly as you want customers to see it - it appears on order confirmation emails - and use a frequently-checked email for the store email address, ideally a branded one (e.g. hello@yourstore.com).
Set the billing/legal business address to the region where the business is registered; the source says this drives which payment and shipping options, plus market behavior, Shopify offers you.

Under Store defaults, set the store currency to your business region (e.g. EUR for a France-registered business) and change currency formatting there; per-market display currencies are managed under Markets and depend on payment gateway availability.
Set the backup region, which is where customers outside your defined markets land by default.
Choose the unit system you personally understand (e.g. kilograms).

If you do not want customers inferring your order volume from order numbers (relevant during large launches), add a prefix or extra digits in the order ID settings so numbers are longer and harder to guess.
caveats: Multi-currency display for foreign customers requires a suitable payment gateway such as Shopify Payments; availability depends on the country where the business is registered (the source notes limitations in some Middle East markets).
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Registering Shopify with your own owner email
cards.summary: Sign up with an email you control so you remain the store owner, then complete payment and business details in one pass.
cards.use_when: You are creating a new Shopify account, possibly with help from an agency or freelancer.
steps: Sign up using your own email, not a contractor's or agency's address; the source stresses that only the store owner can change currencies, delete the store and similar critical actions.
You can start on a personal Gmail, but plan to create a branded email later and use it for customer-facing communication to look more professional.

Complete the payment method step (credit card or PayPal) to start the trial; the source describes Shopify commonly offering something like a short free trial then a heavily discounted first three months.
Fill in business information properly at signup even though it can be edited later - under General settings this drives payment, shipping and market options.
Set your store name when prompted; it can be changed afterward but appears in customer notifications, so choose deliberately.
caveats: Trial length and introductory pricing vary; the source describes seeing seven-day and 14-day trials and roughly three months at $1 in different periods - confirm the current offer.
Business-location restrictions mean some payment features (e.g. Shopify Payments) may not be available in your country.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Using role-based staff permissions instead of blanket access
cards.summary: Add staff users with custom roles scoped to exactly the admin areas they need, and use collaborator access as a cheaper workaround.
cards.use_when: You need to give an employee, contractor or agency access to your Shopify admin without exposing sales figures or settings.
steps: Upgrade to a plan with enough staff seats (the source moved to Grow to add users beyond the Basic limit).
In Settings > Users, add the person's email; they receive a staff invitation to accept.
Instead of a default role, create a custom role: name it, describe it, then tick exact permissions per admin area (home, products, orders, markets, etc.).
Be deliberate about orders access - the source warns that order permissions let the person see your sales numbers, so grant it only where operationally necessary.

If you cannot add a user on your plan, use collaborator access instead: share your myshopify.com domain and collaboration code so the developer or app requests access, then approve them as a collaborator.
Remove access at any time as the store owner.
caveats: Collaborator access is a workaround for the user-seat limit, not a full substitute - the source says at some point most stores genuinely need a paid staff seat, e.g. an order manager.
Admin navigation and permission labels may change; verify in the current Shopify interface.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Connecting a custom domain and handling DNS records
cards.summary: Buy a .com domain early, connect it to Shopify, and learn to add DNS records yourself because future apps will require it.
cards.use_when: You are moving from the default myshopify.com URL to a branded customer-facing domain, or an app asks you to edit DNS records.
steps: Check domain availability when you first choose your brand name - the source warns that later, taken or premium names can be expensive or unavailable.
Prefer the .com for customer familiarity and cross-market recognition; consider also buying other extensions (.co, .au, .de) defensively so nobody else registers your brand name.
Buy either directly through Shopify (simplest, auto-linked to the store) or through a registrar like GoDaddy and use Settings > Domains > Connect existing to link it.
Note that your myshopify.com domain remains important internally - apps and support may ask for it - even though customers should never see it.

If automatic linking is unavailable, log into your registrar, open the domain's Manage DNS section, and add the records the requesting tool specifies: it usually provides type, name and value; the source says most tools require about three records.
Save the records and allow propagation time before testing.
Apply the same DNS-record workflow later for sender emails (Klaviyo, Omnisend) and review apps.
caveats: The source notes it is not certain every registrar behaves identically to GoDaddy; consult the specific provider's DNS interface.
Each DNS tool supplies its own record set - do not copy records between tools.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Setting up store policies and return rules
cards.summary: Generate and customize privacy, terms, shipping, return/refund and contact policies, enable native return rules, and link them in the footer.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to launch or run ads and need legally presentable store policies plus a workable returns process.
steps: In Settings > Policies, use Shopify's insert-template option for each policy (privacy, terms of service, shipping, contact information, terms of sale, legal notice) and then edit the template to match your actual business rather than publishing it untouched.
Configure return rules so customers can initiate returns from their customer account; set the return window and shipping rates in the manage settings.
Keep the shipping policy distinct from actual checkout shipping rates - the source notes rates are configured elsewhere, while the policy communicates how you manage shipping generally.
Link shipping and return/refund policies in the product page where relevant, and all policies in the footer at minimum; the source treats this as required for running ads and for legal coverage.
For contact information, review the auto-filled template - it pulls from your general business details - and edit anything you do not want published (e.g. a personal address).
caveats: The source recommends double-checking policies with a lawyer or legal advisor, especially for the EU and UAE; it flags the UK privacy policy as having different rules.
Shopify's default templates are described as generally good but needing tweaking.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choosing customer support tooling by catalog complexity
cards.summary: Start with the free Shopify Inbox and migrate to AI-assisted support once your catalog or product education demands scale.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how customers will ask pre-purchase questions and how you will answer them at launch versus at scale.
steps: For a new or simple store, install Shopify Inbox: the source describes it as free, with a phone app and a view of each customer's order history so you can reply with context rather than cold.

For large catalogs or education-heavy niches (cosmetics, skincare, electronics) where customers ask many product questions, plan to move to a tool with AI reply features; the source names Gorgias and Tidio as examples.
Use the customer's order and browsing history visible in the inbox to tailor the answer - the source explicitly contrasts context-based replies with random ones.
Before launch, check that contact information is complete in your policies so the support channel is discoverable.
caveats: The source describes the AI option as what you may need later, not a launch requirement; a simple business can run on Shopify Inbox.
Tool names and feature sets change - verify current capabilities and pricing in each tool.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Adding a product: title, description and image ratios
cards.summary: Fill product title/URL, keep the inline description short, and upload all images at one consistent ratio.
cards.use_when: You are creating a product record in Shopify before or alongside PDP design.
steps: Enter the product title. Decide per brand whether to use a clear SEO-friendly name or a branded product name - the source presents both as valid choices.
Save, then check the auto-generated URL at the bottom of the editor; if you later rename the product, return and update the URL handle.

Write a short, simple inline description. Treat it as the text appearing beside the product photos rather than as the whole sales argument - the source says complicated, education-heavy products should get their additional information in a properly structured product page below the fold instead.

Upload all product images in one batch, and keep every image in the same dimensions and ratio across the catalog. The source prefers square because squares cannot mismatch, preventing weird cropping and misalignment.
Keep final image sourcing consistent with the variants you will create (e.g. one set per color).
caveats: Shopify's built-in AI description generator exists in the editor, but the source prefers writing descriptions with ChatGPT; use whichever produces on-brand copy.
The source's short-inline-description guidance is a recommendation, not a hard rule - what determines length is product complexity.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configuring product type, vendor, tags and category
cards.summary: Set type and tags with your future collection filters in mind, and pick a precise Shopify category to unlock extra metafields.
cards.use_when: You are adding products and want collections, filters and product attributes to work without rework.
steps: Set the product Type to the closest descriptive term (e.g. legging, bra, jumpsuit, accessory) - the source notes type feeds collection filters, so specificity now saves cleanup later.
Set the Vendor to the brand name of the item; use the actual third-party brand if you resell other labels.

Use tags as product properties for collection rules, not as social-media-style hashtags. The source's method: decide which collections you intend to build (e.g. 'leggings', 'black leggings') and add tags matching them, because tag-based collection rules are hard to get wrong.

Choose the most precise Shopify product Category via the suggested category. The source shows that a specific category (legging) unlocks an extra attribute section - colors, activewear/clothing features - whereas an uncategorized product shows nothing extra.
Review the auto-detected attribute values (e.g. colors) Shopify pre-fills, then decide which to accept; the source accepted all and noted accuracy was close but not perfect.
Optionally add the product to a collection manually; Shopify places new products in the homepage collection by default and the source considers keeping that acceptable.
caveats: Metafields unlocked by category are not mandatory to fill.
The source describes the category feature as relatively new at recording time; the available attributes per category may have expanded.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Pricing fields: compare-at and cost of goods
cards.summary: Use price, compare-at price and cost per item correctly so discount display works and margin calculations are possible later.
cards.use_when: You are setting product pricing or running a sale and want correct strikethrough display and usable cost data.
steps: In the Pricing section, enter the Price as the amount the customer actually pays today.

To show a sale, enter the original higher amount in Compare at price and the current amount in Price; the source describes the customer seeing the compare-at figure struck through next to the current price.

Enter the per-unit Cost of goods - what you pay for the item itself, not all other expenses. The source cites the example of a €60 selling price with a €20 cost, and stresses that recording cost makes later margin, audit and profitability calculations easier.
Use the 'sell by unit' option only where it applies to your product (the source does not use it for apparel).
caveats: Cost of goods in the source's example excludes other business costs; do not treat it as full landed cost unless you include those.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Independent inventory, SKUs and warehouse coordination
cards.summary: Track inventory in Shopify with SKUs/barcodes so warehouses can match orders accurately, and understand available vs committed vs unavailable.
cards.use_when: You are setting stock levels and identifiers on a product, or preparing to hand fulfillment to a warehouse.
steps: Turn on inventory tracking rather than managing stock only outside Shopify; the source questions the value of switching it off.
Enter the on-hand quantity. Here 'available' is what you can sell; when an order comes in, 'committed' rises and available drops (100 in stock, first order shows committed 1 and available 99).
Use the 'unavailable' quantity field for stock you hold back - damaged items or inventory you do not want publicly sellable - so it is not lost from your records.

Enter at least one of SKU or barcode; the source says most warehouses work adequately with either, and suggests you can even use the same value in both fields. This is how the warehouse identifies what the customer bought and keeps order processing accurate.
If you operate multiple warehouses/locations, each location shows its own quantity field so you can allocate stock per location.
Decide deliberately whether to continue selling when out of stock, based on how quickly you can restock.
caveats: The source describes SKU/barcode importance mainly in the context of third-party warehouse fulfillment.
Inventory location behavior assumes locations are configured; the source covers that setup separately.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Product weight, shipping profile and variants
cards.summary: Record a physical weight so Shopify does not treat the item as digital, and create variants for the option axes customers choose.
cards.use_when: You are completing the shipping section of a product and setting up size/color options for apparel or similar catalog.
steps: In the Shipping section, switch weight on and enter the product weight (the source uses 0.25 in a chosen unit). The source states that leaving weight off makes Shopify treat the item as a digital product, so physical goods need it.
Record weight even if you do not bill shipping by weight: the source notes some warehouses need product weight regardless of your shipping rate method.
Use the customs/duties fields if you ship internationally.
To create variants, click Add options and define the axes; the source's activewear example uses Size (small, medium, large shown, with more needed) and Colour (navy and red).
Expect variants to drive separate media associations and per-variant inventory/pricing where relevant.
caveats: The source's size list in the example is deliberately incomplete for a legging range - build the full size run your catalog needs.
Weight units and the physical/digital determination should be verified in the current Shopify product editor.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Defining brand assets in Shopify settings
cards.summary: Load logo, square logo, colors, cover image, slogan and social links into Store assets so the theme inherits them automatically.
cards.use_when: You are in Settings > General > Store assets and want theme customization to pull consistent branding without manual re-entry.
steps: Upload the rectangular brand logo, then upload a square logo - the source reuses the favicon here because a favicon is square.

Add brand colors by clicking plus and pasting each hex code; define a primary color, a contrasting color chosen to be light against the dark primary for contrast, and secondary colors. The source says brands typically use four to five colors.
Optionally upload a cover image and add a slogan and short business description.
Add social links - at minimum Instagram, TikTok and Facebook. The source observes that people landing on a new brand often check its Instagram next, so missing links cost credibility.
Save. The source emphasizes that defining assets here makes later theme customization easier because the theme draws on these values.
caveats: Cover image, slogan and description are optional in the source's walkthrough.
This step only pays off if your theme is configured to use the store's brand assets; verify in your theme.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Orienting yourself in the Shopify admin navigation
cards.summary: Learn the left-hand admin map so you can find product, order, market and analytics functions without hunting.
cards.use_when: You are new to Shopify admin or onboarding a staff member and need to know where each store operation lives.
steps: Home: Shopify communications and later a sales summary.
Orders: incoming orders and their management.
Products: the product list, plus sub-items for Collections, Inventory, Purchase orders, Transfers and Gift cards.
Customers and Segments: everyone who bought or merely signed up, with segmentation available.
Marketing: campaigns and automations; Discounts sits alongside it.
Content: uploaded files, Menus, Blog posts and Metaobjects (the source flags metaobjects as relevant when creating colour swatches).
Markets: selling internationally to different countries or regions.
Finance and Analytics: analytics becomes important once you have data; the source defers deep coverage to the end of the course.
Sales channels: where you sell; Online Store by default, plus Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Shop once connected.
Apps: third-party apps; and Settings in the corner for all business configuration.
caveats: Admin labels and grouping can change between Shopify releases; verify current navigation.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx
